segments.english: Far be it from you to do such a thing, to kill the righteous with the wicked, so that the righteous and the wicked would be alike. Far be it from you! Will not the Judge of all the earth do justice?
segments.literal: far-be-it to-you from-doing like-the-thing the-this to-kill righteous with wicked and-would-be like-the-righteous like-the-wicked far-be-it to-you will-the-judge-of all the-earth not do justice

tokens.note: Ad profanum, far from the holy. Rashi reads 'profane'; Ibn Ezra reads 'impossible' (see commentary).
The preposition מ on the infinitive is the 'from' of 'far be it from you'.
כ 'like' with דָּבָר, here 'matter, affair'.
Rashi: 'neither this nor anything like it'; the English 'such a thing' covers both.
Hifil infinitive construct of מוּת, 'cause to die, put to death'; the subject is God (Hiph 2).
Indefinite adjective used as a class; the English 'the righteous' is generic.
'together with'.
Generic singular, as 18:25.7.
Weqatal of היה, the consequence of the two infinitives: 'become like'.
Ibn Ezra (and Radak): two כ's together are a short form, 'the righteous like the wicked and the wicked like the righteous'; the English 'alike' follows him.
Etnaḥta on this word divides the verse.
The second exclamation, a reply to the question that follows.
לָּךְ is the pausal form of לְךָ under the zaqef qaton; the data parse it as feminine from the form, but the addressee is the LORD, as in 18:25.2.
Participle with the interrogative he (הֲ). The question is rhetorical; Rashi reads the hataf patah under the he as a sign of astonishment.
Construct: 'the whole of'.

phrases.english: Far be it from you to do such a thing
phrases.literal: 'far-be-it to-you from-doing like-the-thing the-this': the infinitive construct with מ and the noun with כ, rendered 'such a thing'.
'to-kill righteous': the Hifil infinitive and its object, the righteous as a class.
'with wicked': the preposition 'with', here 'together with'.

phrases.english: so that the righteous and the wicked would be alike
phrases.literal: 'and-would-be like-the-righteous like-the-wicked': the weqatal gives the consequence; the paired כ … כ means 'the one like the other' (Ibn Ezra).
'far-be-it to-you': the second exclamation.

phrases.english: Will not the Judge of all the earth do justice
phrases.literal: 'will-the-judge-of all the-earth not do justice': the rhetorical question, with the interrogative he on the participle.

grammar: The two infinitive constructs, מֵעֲשֹׂת and לְהָמִית, depend on חָלִילָה לְךָ: 'far be it from you to do ... to kill'. Each carries its own preposition (מ, ל).

וְהָיָה (18:25.10) is a weqatal after the infinitives and states the result. The paired comparison כַצַּדִּיק כָּרָשָׁע, 'like the righteous, like the wicked', means 'the one like the other' (Ibn Ezra, Radak; compare כָמוֹךָ כְּפַרְעֹה, 44:18).
The question הֲשֹׁפֵט כָּל־הָאָרֶץ (18:25.15) takes the interrogative he. The English puts 'Will not' at the front to make the question clear.
The etnaḥta on כָּרָשָׁע (18:25.12) divides the verse: the first part names the act Abraham calls unthinkable, the second appeals to God's justice. The silluq on מִשְׁפָּט closes it.
לָּךְ (18:25.14) is the pausal form of לְךָ.
segments.note: Both occurrences of חָלִילָה are rendered 'Far be it'. The second opens the appeal, and the English keeps it as a separate sentence.

commentary.summary: Rashi glosses חָלִילָה לְךָ as חֻלִּין הוּא לְךָ, 'it is profane (not holy) for you'. He adds that people would say God's craft is to sweep away all, righteous and wicked alike, as in the flood and the dispersal. The English adopts the sense 'far be it'; the charge itself is not in the English.
Rashi: כַּדָּבָר הַזֶּה means 'not this, and not anything like it' (לֹא הוּא וְלֹא כַּיּוֹצֵא בוֹ). The English 'such a thing' follows this.
Rashi refers the second חָלִילָה לָּךְ to the world to come (לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא). The English does not adopt this temporal reference; it is recorded here.

Rashi: the he of הֲשֹׁפֵט takes a hataf patah and gives the clause an interrogative tone: 'וְכִי מִי שֶׁהוּא שׁוֹפֵט לֹא יַעֲשֶׂה מִשְׁפַּט אֱמֶת', is it possible that a judge would not do true justice? The English is a question.
Ibn Ezra: חָלִלָה is 'a thing that cannot be' (דָּבָר שֶׁלֹּא יִתָּכֵן); some say the word has the sense of חָלוּל, 'hollow, with nothing in it'. The English 'far be it' carries the impossibility.

Ibn Ezra: when two כ's are joined it is a short way of speaking: 'the righteous would be like the wicked, and the wicked like the righteous', as in 'you are like Pharaoh' (44:18), 'as my people, so your people' (1 Kgs 22:4), 'darkness and light are alike' (Ps 139:12). He ends: how could the judge of all the earth not do justice? Radak reads the same. The English 'the righteous and the wicked would be alike' follows.

apparatus: The Hebrew also allows the one-way reading, 'so that the righteous would be like the wicked'; the English follows Ibn Ezra's two-way reading.
context: 'Judge of all the earth' gives the LORD a title that the neighbouring literatures gave to gods of justice: in Mesopotamia the sun god Shamash was invoked as judge of heaven and earth and as guardian of right, and he is shown giving the laws on the stele of Hammurabi. Abraham's appeal rests on the same idea, that the highest judge is bound to judge rightly.

segments.english: The LORD said, "If I find in Sodom fifty righteous people within the city, I will spare the whole place for their sake."
segments.literal: and-said the-LORD if I-find in-Sodom fifty righteous in-midst-of the-city and-I-spare to-all-of the-place for-their-sake

tokens.note: Wayyiqtol, the narrative form that introduces the speech. The LORD's answer is this verse alone; Abraham replies in 18:27.
YHWH, rendered LORD in capitals (decisions: divine names).
Yiqtol 1cs in a conditional clause.
The ב of place with the proper name סְדֹם.
The adjective has no noun in the Hebrew; 'people' is supplied.
Construct of תָּוֶךְ, 'midst'. Ibn Ezra: righteous who fear the LORD openly, in the public life of the city (compare Jer 5:1).
Weqatal 1cs: the consequence of the condition. Qal 3 'take away'; here 'spare'. Radak: the cities and their towns, not destroyed.
לְכָל: 'for all of'.
The place is Sodom itself (Ibn Ezra at 18:29: בִּסְדֹם לְבַדָּהּ). Rashi reads 'all the cities' (see commentary).
בַּ with עָבוּר and the suffix 3mp: 'for the sake of them'.

phrases.literal: 'and-said the-LORD': the wayyiqtol, with the subject after the verb in the Hebrew.
'if I-find in-Sodom': the conditional clause, with the place before the object of the clause.
'fifty righteous': the number and the adjective; the noun is supplied.
'in-midst-of the-city': the construct, 'within the city'.

phrases.english: I will spare the whole place for their sake
phrases.literal: 'and-I-spare to-all-of the-place for-their-sake': the consequence, with the weqatal.

grammar: וַיֹּאמֶר (18:26.1) is a wayyiqtol. It introduces the LORD's answer, which is this verse; Abraham speaks again in 18:27.
The condition is אִם with the yiqtol אֶמְצָא. The consequence is the weqatal וְנָשָׂאתִי: 'if I find ... I will spare'.
The etnaḥta on הָעִיר (18:26.9) divides the verse. The first part is the condition, the second the consequence.
נָשָׂא with לְ of the person or place is 'bear with, forgive': here 'spare'.

commentary.summary: Rashi: 'the whole place' means all the cities (לְכָל הַכְּרַכִּים); Sodom is named because it was the chief city, the most important of them. Ibn Ezra (18:29) rejects the reading that counts the five cities, since the text speaks of Sodom alone; the English 'the whole place' is the city, and Rashi's reading is recorded.

Ibn Ezra: the point of 'within the city' (בְּתוֹךְ הָעִיר) is that they fear the LORD in public (בְּפַרְהֶסְיָא), as in 'roam the streets of Jerusalem' (Jer 5:1). The English 'within the city' carries this; the note on בְּתוֹךְ gives his sense.
Ramban cites Ibn Ezra's 'in public' and prefers his own reading: Abraham said 'within the city' to mean that even foreigners living in it should save it, and he said it for Lot's sake.

context: The site of Sodom has not been identified. Proposals place it at the southern end of the Dead Sea or on the plain north-east of it, near the Jordan; none is agreed.

segments.english: Abraham answered and said, "Now, please, I have been willing to speak to my Lord, though I am dust and ashes.
segments.literal: and-answered Abraham and-said look-pray I-have-been-willing to-speak to-my-Lord and-I dust and-ashes

tokens.note: Wayyiqtol of ענה. The verb opens Abraham's speech; the Hebrew gives no object.
הִנֵּה with נָא: the interjection and the entreaty together; 'Behold' is not used.
Entreaty, as in 18:31 and 18:32.
Hifil perfect 1cs of יָאַל, 'be willing'. The pack lists no sense for the hifil. Rashi and Ibn Ezra both read 'I wished' (רָצִיתִי).
Infinitive construct, piel, with לְ.
Qamats: the address is to God, 'my Lord' (decisions, Genesis 18-50).
The ו sets the clause in contrast: 'though I am dust and ashes'.
The pair is the formula of abasement before God.

phrases.literal: 'and-answered Abraham and-said': the two wayyiqtol forms open the speech.
'look-pray': the interjection with the entreaty; 'now' for the sense.

phrases.english: I have been willing to speak
phrases.literal: 'I-have-been-willing to-speak': the hifil perfect followed by the infinitive.
'to-my-Lord': the address to God.

phrases.english: though I am dust and ashes
phrases.literal: 'and-I dust and-ashes': a verbless clause, the English supplies 'am'.

grammar: וַיַּעַן (18:27.1) and וַיֹּאמַר (18:27.3) are two wayyiqtol forms. Together they open the speech, which runs on into 18:28.
הוֹאַלְתִּי is a hifil qatal 1cs of יָאַל. Rashi and Ibn Ezra take it as 'I wished', the English 'I have been willing'.
הִנֵּה־נָא is an interjection with an entreaty: 'look, please'. The English 'Now, please' keeps both.
וְאָנֹכִי עָפָר וָאֵפֶר is verbless: 'and I dust and ashes'. The ו is contrastive, and the English supplies 'am'.

commentary.summary: Rashi: הוֹאַלְתִּי means רָצִיתִי, 'I wanted', as in וַיּוֹאֶל מֹשֶׁה (Exod 2:21). The English 'I have been willing' is this sense.

Rashi: 'I deserved already to be dust at the hands of kings and ashes at the hands of Nimrod, but for your mercy which stood for me.' The English gives the plain abasement; Rashi's history is recorded here.

Ibn Ezra: הוֹאַלְתִּי is not 'I began' (הַחִלּוֹתִי, as Onkelos שָׁרֵיתִי); it means only 'I wished' (רָצִיתִי), as in הוֹאִיל מֹשֶׁה (Deut 1:5). The כ of אָנֹכִי is added, or אֲנִי and אָנֹכִי are two words with one meaning. The English 'I have been willing' follows.

Ibn Ezra: 'I am dust and ashes' means 'I was dust and to ashes I shall return'; the chief point is the foundation of the body, that is, the bones. The English 'dust and ashes' follows this plain sense.

context: Dust and ashes belong to the rites of mourning and self-abasement known across the ancient Near East: mourners strewed dust on their heads and sat in ashes, as El does on hearing of Baal's death in the Ugaritic Baal cycle. Abraham names himself by the stuff of those rites.

segments.english: Perhaps the fifty righteous will be five short. Will you destroy the whole city for the lack of five?" He said, "I will not destroy if I find there forty-five."
segments.literal: perhaps will-be-lacking fifty the-righteous five will-you-destroy for-five [obj] the-whole-of the-city and-he-said not I-will-destroy if I-find there forty and-five

tokens.note: Yiqtol 3mp of חָסֵר with paragogic nun, intransitive: 'be lacking'. Ibn Ezra: 'perhaps a tenth of the number will be lacking'.
The five that are lacking from the fifty.
Interrogative he with yiqtol 2ms: 'will you destroy?' Abraham addresses God.
בְּ 'because of': the five who are missing (Ibn Ezra).
The object marker אֵת has no English counterpart.
The LORD's reply begins here.
Yiqtol 1cs.
The ו joins 'and five': forty-five.

phrases.english: Perhaps the fifty righteous will be five short
phrases.literal: 'perhaps will-be-lacking fifty the-righteous five': the doubt is expressed by אוּלַי with yiqtol.
'will-you-destroy': the interrogative he with the hifil yiqtol 2ms.
'for-five': the preposition ב, 'because of the five'.
'[obj] the-whole-of the-city': the object marker is not rendered.
'and-he-said': the wayyiqtol, the LORD's reply.
'not I-will-destroy': the negative with the hifil yiqtol 1cs.
'if I-find there': the conditional.
'forty and-five': the sum of the two numerals.

grammar: הֲתַשְׁחִית (18:28.6) is the interrogative he with the hifil yiqtol 2ms of שָׁחַת. The question is Abraham's protest, addressed to God.
יַחְסְרוּן is Qal 2 'be lacking': five are missing from the fifty. The construction with אוּלַי (perhaps) expresses doubt; Abraham does not assert that five are lacking.
The etnaḥta on הָעִיר (18:28.10) closes Abraham's question. The reply, וַיֹּאמֶר (18:28.11), begins God's answer.
Abraham's speech begins in 18:27 and runs through 18:28, so the English opens the quotation in 18:27 and closes it after 'five?'.

commentary.summary: Rashi: forty-five are nine for each of the five cities, and you, the Righteous One of the world, will join them as the tenth. Ibn Ezra (18:29) rejects the count by the five cities, since the text speaks of Sodom alone; the English keeps the plain question about the five who are lacking.
Ibn Ezra: 'perhaps a tenth of the number will be lacking' (אוּלַי תֶּחְסַר עֲשִׂירִית מֵהַמִּסְפָּר): five is a tenth of fifty. The English 'five short' is this.

Ibn Ezra: 'will you destroy for five' means 'because of the five who will be lacking, (will you destroy) the whole?' Then Abraham said, 'perhaps a ninth of the number I named will be lacking' (five of forty-five, 18:29), and God answered that if they are found there he will not destroy them. The English 'for the lack of five' is this reading.

segments.english: He spoke to him again and said, "Perhaps forty will be found there." He said, "I will not do it for the sake of the forty."
segments.literal: and-added again to-speak to-him and-said perhaps will-be-found there forty and-said not I-will-do for-the-sake-of the-forty

tokens.note: Wayyiqtol hifil of יָסַף with the infinitive that follows: 'added to speak', 'went on again'.
The adverb עוֹד goes with the verb in 18:29.1.
Nifal yiqtol 3mp with paragogic nun, 'will be found'; the subject is אַרְבָּעִים, 'forty'.
The first of the successive numbers: forty, thirty, twenty, ten.
The LORD's reply.
Yiqtol 1cs. The object, destruction, is supplied from the context (Ibn Ezra).
בַּ with עָבוּר: 'for the sake of'.

phrases.literal: 'and-added again to-speak to-him': the hifil wayyiqtol with the infinitive, 'went on to speak to him again'.
'and-said perhaps': the verb of speech and the particle of doubt that opens the proposal.
'will-be-found there forty': the nifal, the number last.
'and-he-said not I-will-do': the LORD's answer.

phrases.english: for the sake of the forty
phrases.literal: 'for-the-sake-of the-forty': the reason for the refusal.

grammar: וַיֹּסֶף עוֹד לְדַבֵּר is a hifil wayyiqtol of יָסַף with an infinitive: 'went on to speak'. The English gives the adverb 'again'.
אוּלַי with the nifal yiqtol יִמָּצְאוּן is a proposal: 'perhaps forty will be found there'. The numeral אַרְבָּעִים, after the verb, is its subject.
The answer is לֹא with the yiqtol אֶעֱשֶׂה. The object, destruction, is not written; the English 'I will not do it' keeps the Hebrew's ellipsis.
The etnaḥta on אַרְבָּעִים (18:29.9) divides the verse at Abraham's proposal; the answer follows.
segments.note: The English keeps 'do it' for the ellipsis. Ibn Ezra makes the object 'destruction' explicit (commentary).

commentary.summary: Rashi: forty would save four of the cities, thirty three, twenty two, and ten one. Ibn Ezra rejects any count by the five cities, since the text speaks of Sodom alone; the English keeps the plain sense, forty righteous people in Sodom.

Ibn Ezra: 'I will not do' means 'I will not do destruction'. After the tenth and the ninth, Abraham did not go on joining the two lacks, but asked next for a quarter, a third and a half to be lacking (forty to thirty, twenty, ten). Some say he went no lower than ten because there would be two in each of the five cities; this is not right, since he said 'in Sodom' alone. Though the sages taught that there is no public prayer with fewer than ten, this verse too supports that tradition. The English 'I will not do it' follows.

segments.english: Abraham said, "Please, let not my Lord be angry, and let me speak. Perhaps thirty will be found there." He said, "I will not do it if I find thirty there."
segments.literal: and-said not please let-it-burn to-my-Lord and-let-me-speak perhaps will-be-found there thirty and-said not I-will-do if I-find there thirty

tokens.note: The speaker is Abraham; the verse begins a new speech after the LORD's reply.
The negative אַל with a jussive: 'let not'.
Entreaty; with אַל it softens the request.
Jussive qal 3ms of חָרָה, 'burn', used impersonally with לְ of the person: 'let it not burn to my Lord', that is, 'let not my Lord be angry'.
Qamats: the address is to God (decisions, Genesis 18-50).
Cohortative piel 1cs of דָּבַר: 'let me speak'.
The LORD's reply.
As at 18:29: the sense is 'I will not destroy'.

phrases.literal: 'and-said let-not please': the speaker, then the negative and the entreaty.
'be-angry to-my-Lord': the jussive, the address to God.
'and-let-me-speak': the cohortative.

phrases.english: Perhaps thirty will be found there
phrases.literal: 'perhaps will-be-found there thirty': the proposal.

phrases.english: He said, I will not do
phrases.literal: 'and-he-said not I-will-do': the LORD's answer.
'if I-find there thirty': the conditional.

grammar: וַאֲדַבֵּרָה is a cohortative: 'let me speak'. The cohortative after the jussive makes Abraham's request a double petition.
יִחַר is a jussive after אַל: 'let not ... be angry'. God is addressed as 'my Lord'.
The request repeats 18:29 with thirty in place of forty. The answer repeats too, 'I will not do it', and the English keeps the parallel.
The etnaḥta on שְׁלֹשִׁים (18:30.10) divides the verse: Abraham's plea and proposal come first; God's reply follows.

commentary.summary: Radak: Abraham says 'let not my Lord be angry' out of fear that the judgment before God be too heavy, and so he shortened the fifties to tens. This is his motive; it does not change the English.

segments.english: Abraham said, "Now, please, I have been willing to speak to my Lord. Perhaps twenty will be found there." He said, "I will not destroy for the sake of the twenty."
segments.literal: and-said look-pray I-have-been-willing to-speak to-my-Lord perhaps will-be-found there twenty and-said not I-will-destroy for-the-sake-of the-twenty

tokens.note: Abraham again; the wayyiqtol opens the next speech.
הִנֵּה with נָא: 'look, please', as at 18:27.
Hifil perfect 1cs of יָאַל; the pack lists no sense for the hifil. See 18:27.
Qamats: God (decisions, Genesis 18-50).
The LORD's reply.
Yiqtol 1cs.
בַּ with עָבוּר.

phrases.literal: 'and-said look-pray': the speaker, then the interjection with the entreaty.

phrases.english: I have been willing to speak
phrases.literal: 'I-have-been-willing to-speak'.
'to-my-Lord': the address to God.

phrases.english: Perhaps twenty will be found there
phrases.literal: 'perhaps will-be-found there twenty': the proposal.

phrases.english: He said, I will not destroy
phrases.literal: 'and-he-said not I-will-destroy': the LORD's answer.

phrases.english: for the sake of the twenty
phrases.literal: 'for-the-sake-of the-twenty'.

grammar: The speech repeats the form of 18:27 with 'twenty' in place of forty: Abraham lowers the number again by ten.
The hifil of יָאַל is as in 18:27, 'I have been willing'.
The LORD's reply uses לֹא with the hifil yiqtol אַשְׁחִית: 'I will not destroy'.
The etnaḥta on עֶשְׂרִים (18:31.11) divides the verse; the second half is God's reply.

commentary.summary: Rashi: הוֹאַלְתִּי means רָצִיתִי, 'I wished', as in וַיּוֹאֶל מֹשֶׁה. The English 'I have been willing' is this sense.

segments.english: Abraham said, "Please, let not my Lord be angry, and let me speak only this once. Perhaps ten will be found there." He said, "I will not destroy for the sake of the ten."
segments.literal: and-said not please let-it-burn to-my-Lord and-let-me-speak only the-time perhaps will-be-found there ten and-said not I-will-destroy for-the-sake-of the-ten

tokens.note: Abraham speaks.
The negative אַל with a jussive.
Jussive qal 3ms of חָרָה, impersonal, as at 18:30.
Qamats: God.
Cohortative piel 1cs of דָּבַר.
אַךְ, here restrictive: 'only'. The pack's entry shows only its first sense, 'surely'; BDB also gives the restrictive 'only'.
הַפַּעַם, 'the time': 'this once'.
The last number in the bargaining.
The LORD's reply.
Yiqtol 1cs.
בַּ with עָבוּר.

phrases.literal: 'and-said let-not please': the speaker, then the negative and the entreaty.
'be-angry to-my-Lord': the jussive, the address to God.

phrases.english: and let me speak only this once
phrases.literal: 'and-let-me-speak only the-once': the cohortative, with the restriction to one more attempt.

phrases.english: Perhaps ten will be found there
phrases.literal: 'perhaps will-be-found there ten': the last proposal.

phrases.english: He said, I will not destroy
phrases.literal: 'and-he-said not I-will-destroy': the LORD's answer.

phrases.english: for the sake of the ten
phrases.literal: 'for-the-sake-of the-ten'.

grammar: This is Abraham's last request: ten. In 18:33 the LORD goes his way and the dialogue ends.
אַךְ הַפַּעַם, 'only this once', restricts the request; אַךְ is restrictive here.
The jussive יִחַר and the cohortative וַאֲדַבְּרָה repeat the petition of 18:30 without change.
The etnaḥta on עֲשָׂרָה (18:32.12) divides the verse: Abraham's request and proposal come first; the LORD's reply follows.

commentary.summary: Rashi: Abraham did not ask for fewer than ten. In the generation of the flood there were eight (Noah, his sons and their wives), and they did not save their generation; for nine, with God joined to them, he had already asked and found none. Ibn Ezra (18:29) gives another account of the steps and ties the ten to the rule of ten for public prayer; the English stops at ten, as the text does.
